proposal: Attack the hidden reflection in the dihedral group D_N by preparing many single-qubit coset states labeled by random elements of Z_N, then repeatedly pairing registers whose labels agree in their low-order bits and combining them so those bits cancel, until a state exposing one bit of the hidden slope remains. Iterating bit by bit should find the hidden reflection with time and number of oracle calls both exp(O(sqrt(log N))), and the same sieve should also handle hidden shift instances on any finitely generated abelian group.
quote: We present a quantum algorithm for the dihedral hidden subgroup problem with time and query complexity

proposal: For the Boolean hidden shift problem where the known function f is bent and belongs to a standard family whose dual bent function is efficiently computable (for example Maiorana-McFarland functions), query the phase oracle of the shifted function on a uniform superposition, apply the Hadamard transform, apply the phase oracle of the dual function, and apply the Hadamard transform again. This should output the n-bit shift in polynomial time using O(1) queries, while classical algorithms need exponentially many queries.
quote: solve the hidden shift problems for several well-known classes of bent functions in polynomial time and with a constant number of queries

proposal: Take an oracle g(j, y), with 0 <= j < M and y in Z_N, promised to satisfy g(j, y) = g(j+1, y+s) whenever j+1 < M; this interpolates between an abelian problem when M = N and the dihedral problem when M = 2. If M is at least N^eps for a fixed eps > 0, implementing the pretty good measurement on the resulting states, with Lenstra's fixed-dimension integer programming algorithm as a classical subroutine, should recover s in time poly(log N).
quote: we give an efficient (i.e., poly(log N)) quantum algorithm for this problem provided M > N^epsilon

proposal: Given oracle access to the shifted quadratic character x -> chi(x+s) over a finite field F_q, load these values as phases, apply the quantum Fourier transform over F_q, and remove the resulting chi-dependent phase, which can be computed without the oracle because the Legendre symbol is nearly its own Fourier transform. This should recover s exactly with two oracle calls in total, whereas a classical randomized procedure needs about log q queries.
quote: the unknown s in F_q can be obtained exactly with only two quantum calls to f_s

proposal: For hidden subgroup problems on groups (Z_p)^r semidirect Z_p with r held fixed, the Heisenberg group being r = 2, measure several hidden subgroup states jointly with the pretty good measurement. Its success probability and circuit implementation reduce to an average-case algebraic equation-solving problem, and solving that problem efficiently should give a poly(log p) quantum algorithm for these nonabelian cases, showing that entangled multi-copy measurements help.
quote: we find efficient quantum algorithms for a number of nonabelian hidden subgroup problems, including some for which no efficient algorithm was previously known: certain metacyclic groups as well as all groups of the form (Z_p)^r X| Z_p for fixed r

proposal: Generalize Simon's problem to G^n for a fixed nonabelian group G of constant size: the oracle hides an involution whose n coordinates are each trivial or conjugate to a fixed known element k, and G has a character chi with chi(k) = -chi(1). Combining a Kuperberg-style sieve over many coset states with a missing-harmonic test should recover the hidden involution in time exp(O(sqrt(n log n))).
quote: Here we give quantum algorithms with time complexity 2^O(sqrt(n log n)) that recover hidden involutions

proposal: For the hidden subgroup problem over an arbitrary finite group, with the hidden subgroup promised to lie in a known candidate family H, apply the pretty good measurement to O(log|H|) independent coset states. This should identify the hidden subgroup with bounded error, and when all candidates share the same prime order p the number of coset states needed should be Theta(log|H| / log p) for both the identification and decision versions.
quote: This shows that the pretty good measurement can identify any hidden subgroup of an arbitrary group with at most

proposal: Treat the hidden polynomial problem as a hidden symmetry subgroup problem: a group acts on a set, the oracle's level sets partition it, and the target is the subgroup of symmetries preserving that partition. Reducing this symmetry problem to an ordinary hidden subgroup problem should solve the hidden polynomial problem efficiently on a quantum computer when the hidden polynomials are multivariate quadratics over a field of constant characteristic.
quote: we obtain the first efficient quantum algorithm for the hidden polynomial problem for multivariate quadratic polynomials over fields of constant characteristic

proposal: For two linear codes of length n over any field whose hulls are trivial with respect to some inner product, compute from each code a basis-independent n x n matrix (the projection onto the code, which exists because the hull is trivial and costs one matrix inversion) and read it as a weighted graph on the n coordinates. An isomorphism test for these weighted graphs should then decide deterministically whether the codes are permutation equivalent, so this case reduces efficiently to graph isomorphism.
quote: one may deterministically decide the permutation code equivalence provided that the underlying vector spaces intersect trivially with their orthogonal complement

proposal: For F_{q^m}-linear codes in the rank metric, map code equivalence to the right-equivalence problem for matrix codes, and solve the latter with linear algebra plus polynomial factorization over finite fields, handling codes with nontrivial stabilizer algebras via Wedderburn-Artin structure theory. This should place the problem in P or in ZPP, depending on how large the ground field is.
quote: We prove the latter problem to be either in $\mathcal{P}$ or in $\mathcal{ZPP}$ depending of the ground field size

proposal: Given two k-dimensional matrix codes C and D inside F_q^{m x n}, find invertible P and Q with D = P C Q^{-1} by first reducing to the conjugacy case P = Q, then using an invariant built from the hull of the code together with a birthday-style list collision. This should solve the general problem, and for k = m = n match the roughly q^{k/2} running time of the best earlier cubic-case method while using less memory.
quote: We present a novel algorithm which solves the problem in the general case

proposal: Encode a unique-SVP instance into dihedral coset states so that a coset-sampling solver for the dihedral hidden subgroup problem recovers the shortest vector, then handle that dihedral problem with an algorithm for subset sum on random instances. Chaining the two steps should give a quantum reduction from unique-SVP with gap Theta(n^{2.5}) to average-case subset sum.
quote: we get a quantum reduction from $Θ(n^{2.5})$-unique-SVP to the average case subset sum problem

proposal: Apply a filtering step to LWE-like quantum states, i.e. superpositions over samples with polynomial modulus and errors drawn from bounded-uniform or Laplace distributions, to solve LWE from such states in polynomial time. Feeding this into existing quantum reductions should give polynomial-time quantum algorithms for SIS in the infinity norm when the matrix is very wide, the prime modulus q is polynomial in size, and the norm bound is q/2 minus a constant, and also for extrapolated DCP at certain parameters.
quote: Our main contribution is solving LWE given LWE-like quantum states with interesting parameters using a filtering technique

proposal: Define a relaxed dihedral coset problem in which each sample is a superposition over several consecutive multiples of the secret shift, weighted by an amplitude profile, instead of just two points. Quantum polynomial-time reductions in both directions should show that LWE is equivalent to this relaxed problem, with the amount of extrapolation set by the LWE noise rate, generalizing the classic implication that a polynomial-time DCP algorithm yields one for LWE.
quote: under quantum polynomial time reductions, LWE is equivalent to a relaxed version of the dihedral coset problem

proposal: To find a marked item among N unsorted entries given only a membership oracle, start from the uniform superposition and alternate a phase flip on the marked item with inversion about the mean. After about (pi/4) sqrt(N) rounds the marked item should be measured with high probability, so search takes O(sqrt(N)) oracle steps, compared with roughly N/2 for any classical method.
quote: the desired phone number can be obtained in only O(sqrt(N)) steps

proposal: In oracle identification, an unknown n-bit string is promised to belong to a known set C of size M, and only its individual bits can be queried. A quantum query algorithm should identify the string using O(sqrt(n * log M / (1 + log(n / log M)))) queries.
quote: We develop a quantum query algorithm for this problem with query complexity

proposal: For the hidden subgroup problem over any finite group G, query the oracle to build polynomially many (in log|G|) coset states and then run an error-free procedure that pins down the subgroup, without regard to computational cost. This should identify the hidden subgroup with certainty using poly(log|G|) oracle calls, even though the processing time stays exponential.
quote: identifies with certainty a hidden subgroup of an arbitrary finite group G in only a polynomial

proposal: Use the quantum Fourier transform to turn an optimization problem over a finite field into a decoding problem: prepare a superposition weighted by a polynomial in the objective, which requires uncomputing an error register by syndrome decoding of a code defined by the constraint matrix, then Fourier-transform. For the problem of fitting a low-degree polynomial over a finite field to as many given target sets as possible, the decoding step is Reed-Solomon decoding, which is efficient, so the method should reach, in polynomial time, approximation levels for which the best known classical algorithms need superpolynomial time.
quote: For approximating optimal polynomial fits over finite fields, DQI achieves a superpolynomial speedup over known classical algorithms

proposal: Relative to a random oracle, define an NP search problem whose solutions are codewords of a suitable error-correcting code that satisfy oracle-defined conditions, and solve it with a quantum algorithm that combines the Fourier transform with efficient decoding of the code. This should give an unconditional quantum advantage for an NP search problem: quantum polynomial time solves it while classical probabilistic polynomial time does not, without relying on algebraic structure in the oracle.
quote: There are NP search problems solvable by quantum polynomial-time machines but not classical probabilistic polynomial-time machines

proposal: Approximately scale a tensor of any format to prescribed one-body marginals by alternating minimization, using highest-weight vectors of the relevant group representations as potential functions to bound progress. This should run in polynomial time whenever scaling is possible, decide weak membership in the associated moment polytopes efficiently, and in particular solve the one-body quantum marginal problem efficiently.
quote: We present a polynomial time algorithm to approximately scale tensors of any format to arbitrary prescribed marginals

proposal: Reduce factoring an integer N to finding the multiplicative order of a random base modulo N, and find that order on a quantum computer by applying the quantum Fourier transform to a superposition of modular exponentiations; handle discrete logarithms the same way as a two-dimensional period-finding problem. Both should take time polynomial in the bit length of the input.
quote: Efficient randomized algorithms are given for these two problems on a hypothetical quantum computer

proposal: Pose a black-box traversal problem on two balanced binary trees glued together at their leaves by a random cycle, with vertex names hidden behind an oracle, where the task is to reach the exit root from the entrance root. A continuous-time quantum walk started at the entrance and implemented efficiently from the oracle should reach the exit in polynomial time, an exponential speedup over classical algorithms.
quote: We construct an oracular (i.e., black box) problem that can be solved exponentially faster on a quantum computer than on a classical computer

proposal: Prove an adiabatic theorem for discrete-time walk operators whose error bound depends on the spectral gap, and use it to move from an easy initial state to the solution state of a block-encoded linear system Ax = b. This should solve the quantum linear systems problem with O(kappa log(1/eps)) queries, strictly linear in the condition number kappa and optimal jointly in kappa and the precision eps.
quote: We use this discrete adiabatic theorem to develop a quantum algorithm for solving linear systems that is asymptotically optimal

proposal: For random quantum circuits in the anticoncentration regime where each gate suffers noise at a fixed constant rate, expand the output distribution in Pauli paths and keep only the low-weight paths, since noise damps the others. This classical procedure should sample from the noisy circuit's output distribution with total variation error 1/poly(n) in polynomial time.
quote: We give a polynomial time classical algorithm for sampling from the output distribution of a noisy random quantum circuit in the regime of anti-concentration
